docs.title: CLI Overview
docs.text:
milk compiles into multiple executables:

  • milk-cli: The interactive command line interface (CLI). Running it starts a prompt from which all module functions can be launched. Type m? to list loaded modules and their commands.
  • milk-fpsexec-*: Standalone executables for individual compute units. Each runs a single FPS-enabled function in isolation, managed via tmux and milk-fpsCTRL.

The source code is organized in modules. A module includes C code and documentation. It may also include data files, scripts, and extended documentation.

For more details see the Programmer's Guide.

← Documentation Index

docs.title: Command Line Interface Syntax
docs.text:
The interactive CLI is provided by the milk-cli executable (typically aliased as milk). Source code is in src/cli/CLIcore/.

Note

Standalone executables (milk-fpsexec-*) have their own command-line interfaces. See FPS Standalone Modes.

See also: FPS · Streams · FAQ · Build Tiers

docs.title: Starting & Configuring
docs.text: This section covers launching milk-cli, configuring its behavior, and loading additional modules.

docs.title: Command-Line Options
docs.text:
When launching milk-cli, the following arguments are available:

Option Description -h, --help Print help and exit -i, --info Print version, settings, info and exit --verbose Be verbose -d, --debug=LEVEL Set debug level at startup -o, --overwrite Auto-overwrite FITS files (use with caution) -e, --errorexit Exit on command error -l, --listimf Write image list to imlist.txt -m, --mmon=TTY Open memory monitor on tty device -n, --pname=NAME Rename process -p, --priority=PR Set RT priority (0–99, higher = higher) -f, --fifoflag Enable fifo input; auto-generate fifo path -F, --fifoname=PATH Enable fifo input; use custom fifo path -s, --startup=FILE Feed startup file into fifo (requires -f or -F) -A, --autocomplete Enable autocomplete preview --no-autocomplete Disable autocomplete --no-history-suggest Disable ghost history suggestions --no-arg-hints Disable argument hint bar --no-fuzzy Disable fuzzy matching in completions

Examples:

$ milk-cli -m /dev/tty2            # memory monitor on tty2
$ milk-cli -p 90                   # high RT priority
$ milk-cli -f                      # enable fifo (auto-named)
$ milk-cli -F /tmp/myfifo          # enable fifo, custom path
$ milk-cli -F /tmp/myfifo -s init.milk  # fifo + startup script

docs.title: Startup Script
docs.text:
Commands in ~/.milkrc are executed line-by-line on startup. Blank lines and # comments are skipped.

# Example ~/.milkrc
alias li mem.listim
synhl on

docs.title: Configurable Prompt
docs.text:
Customize the prompt format using setprompt:

milk-cli > setprompt "%u@%h %d > "
user@host src >
Token Expands to %h hostname %u username %d current directory basename %t HH:MM:SS %n process name

docs.title: Module Loading
docs.text:
Load shared library modules at runtime:

milk-cli > soload mylib.so         # load shared object
milk-cli > mload COREMOD_arith     # load module by name

docs.title: Input & Editing
docs.text: The CLI provides a rich interactive editing experience with tab completion, inline suggestions, and syntax highlighting — all built on GNU readline.

docs.title: Syntax Rules
docs.text:
• Spaces separate arguments (count doesn't matter)
  • Comments follow #
  • Unrecognized input is interpreted as arithmetic
milk-cli > <command> <arg1> <arg2>   # comment

docs.title: Tab Completion
docs.text:
• First argument: matches command → image → filename
  • Additional arguments: context-aware based on command's parameter types:
  • FILENAME / FITSFILENAME args → filesystem paths
  • FPSNAME args → scan /dev/shm/fps.*.shm entries
  • Other args → match image stream names
  • Fuzzy (substring) matching automatically kicks in when prefix matching finds nothing
milk-cli > mem.<TAB>           # list commands starting with mem.
milk-cli > iofits.loadfits my<TAB>    # complete filename

docs.title: Ghost Suggestions
docs.text: As you type, a dim "ghost" suggestion appears inline based on your command history. Press the right arrow key to accept it.

docs.title: Argument Hints
docs.text: When a known command is typed, the bottom line shows the command's syntax with <angle bracket> parameter tokens. The active argument position is highlighted in bold cyan, advancing as you type each argument.

docs.title: Readline Editing
docs.text:
GNU readline is used for line editing. Type helprl at the prompt for a quick reference. See GNU readline documentation.

Key bindings include Ctrl+A (start of line), Ctrl+E (end of line), Ctrl+R (reverse history search), and arrow keys for navigation.

docs.title: Backslash Line Continuation
docs.text:
End a line with \ to continue on the next line. The prompt changes to > for continuation lines:

milk-cli > arith.imfunc \
>   im1 im2 outim

docs.title: Syntax Highlighting
docs.text:
The first word is colored green (valid command) or red (unknown). Toggle with:

milk-cli > synhl off             # disable
milk-cli > synhl on              # enable (default)

Tip

If you encounter rendering issues with syntax highlighting, disable it with synhl off.

docs.title: Auto-Correction
docs.text:
When a command is not found, the CLI suggests the closest match using Levenshtein distance:

milk-cli > mem.lisim
Command 'mem.lisim' not found. Did you mean 'mem.listim'?

docs.title: Help & Discovery
docs.text: Several commands help you explore the available commands and modules.

docs.title: Help Commands
docs.text:
milk-cli > ?                       # print help
milk-cli > help                    # same as ?
milk-cli > helprl                  # readline quick reference
milk-cli > lm?                     # list all loaded modules
milk-cli > m? <module>             # list commands for a module
milk-cli > m?                      # list commands for all modules
milk-cli > cmd? <command>          # detailed command description
milk-cli > cmd?                    # describe all commands
milk-cli > cmdinfo? <pattern>      # search command info by regex

Command names and descriptions are color-coded: cyan for command names, green for descriptions, yellow for examples, dim for source file paths.

docs.title: Important Commands
docs.text:
milk-cli > ci                      # compilation info & memory usage
milk-cli > mem.listim              # list all images in memory
milk-cli > listimf <file>          # list images, write to file
milk-cli > !<syscmd>               # execute system command
milk-cli > quit                    # exit (or: exit, exitCLI)
milk-cli > mem.mk2Dim <im> <xs> <ys>   # create 2D image
milk-cli > usleep <usec>           # sleep for <usec> microseconds
milk-cli > dpsingle                # set default precision to float
milk-cli > dpdouble                # set default precision to double
milk-cli > cd <dir>                # change current working directory
milk-cli > pwd                     # print current working directory

docs.title: History
docs.text: The CLI maintains both readline history (for arrow-key recall) and a persistent log of every command with timestamps and session IDs.

docs.title: Persistent History
docs.text:
Command history is saved to ~/.milk_history and loaded at startup. Up to 1000 entries are retained between sessions.

milk-cli > ghistory              # show last 20 entries (all sessions)
milk-cli > ghistory 50           # show last 50 entries
milk-cli > lhistory              # show entries from current session

Use Ctrl+R for interactive reverse search through history.

docs.title: History Expansion
docs.text:
Shortcut Description !! Re-run the last command !! args Append args to the last command !$ Insert the last argument of the previous command !prefix Re-run the last command starting with prefix

The expanded command is printed with a >> prefix before execution.

milk-cli > iofits.loadfits im1.fits im1
milk-cli > !!                   # re-runs: iofits.loadfits im1.fits im1
milk-cli > iofits.save_fl !$    # expands to: iofits.save_fl im1

docs.title: Fuzzy History Search
docs.text:
milk-cli > searchhist mem.listim

Finds all history entries containing "mem.listim" (case- insensitive) and highlights the matching substring in yellow. Shows match count at the end.

docs.title: Command Statistics
docs.text:
milk-cli > cmdstats              # top 20 most-used commands

Shows command name and call count for the current session.

docs.title: Session Logging
docs.text:
Log all executed commands with timestamps:

milk-cli > sessionlog on          # log to ~/.milk_session.log
milk-cli > sessionlog mylog.txt   # log to custom file
milk-cli > sessionlog off         # stop logging

Each entry includes a timestamp and elapsed time since the session started.

docs.title: Shell Features
docs.text: The CLI supports many shell-like features: scripting, chaining, piping, redirection, environment variable expansion, and arithmetic.

docs.title: Script Execution
docs.text:
milk-cli > source myscript.milk  # run commands from file
milk-cli > . myscript.milk       # same thing (dot-source)

Blank lines and # comments are skipped. On error, the filename and line number are printed in red.

The CLI supports bash-like scripting constructs including variables, arithmetic, flow control (if/while/for), and user-defined functions. See the Scripting page for full documentation.

Command Description source <file> Execute a script file . <file> Same as source (dot-source) savescript <file> Save variables and functions to file savehistory <file> Save command history to file

docs.title: Command Timing
docs.text:
milk-cli > time mem.listim      # measure execution time

Prints the elapsed wall-clock time after the command completes.

docs.title: Command Chaining
docs.text:
Sequential, conditional, and unconditional chaining:

milk-cli > cmd1 ; cmd2         # always run cmd2 after cmd1
milk-cli > cmd1 && cmd2        # run cmd2 only if cmd1 succeeds
milk-cli > cmd1 || cmd2        # run cmd2 only if cmd1 fails

Operators inside double-quoted strings are not treated as chain separators.

docs.title: Pipe to Shell
docs.text:
Pipe a CLI command's output to a standard shell command:

milk-cli > mem.listim | grep wfs     # filter image list
milk-cli > cmd? | head -5            # show first 5 help lines

docs.title: Output Redirect
docs.text:
Redirect command output to a file:

milk-cli > mem.listim > imlist.txt  # write image list to file

docs.title: Environment Variable Expansion
docs.text:
$VAR and ${VAR} are expanded before execution:

milk-cli > iofits.loadfits ${HOME}/data/im.fits im1
milk-cli > iofits.saveFITS im1 $OUTDIR/result.fits

docs.title: Command Substitution
docs.text:
Replace $(cmd) or `cmd` in the command line with the standard output of the command execution.

milk-cli > cd $(echo /tmp)
milk-cli > iofits.loadfits `findim.sh` result

docs.title: Wildcard Expansion (Globbing)
docs.text:
File path wildcards like *, ?, and [] are automatically expanded into matching files if placed unquoted in arguments.

milk-cli > iofits.imgs2cube *.fits cube.fits

docs.title: Arithmetic Operations
docs.text:
Expressions not matching any command are evaluated as image arithmetic:

milk-cli > im1=sqrt(im+2.0)       # arithmetic on images

docs.title: Watch Command
docs.text:
milk-cli > watch 1000 mem.listim   # repeat every 1000ms

Press any key to stop the repeating execution.

docs.title: Customization
docs.text: The CLI supports aliases and bookmarks for frequently-used commands.

docs.title: Command Aliases
docs.text:
milk-cli > alias li mem.listim   # create alias
milk-cli > unalias li            # remove alias
milk-cli > aliases               # list all aliases

Aliases persist in ~/.milk_aliases.

docs.title: Command Bookmarks
docs.text:
Save and recall multi-command sequences:

milk-cli > bookmark save setup "cmd1 ; cmd2 ; cmd3"
milk-cli > bookmark run setup
milk-cli > bookmark list
milk-cli > bookmark rm setup

Bookmarks persist in ~/.milk_bookmarks.

docs.title: External Integration
docs.text: The CLI integrates with external processes and standard Linux tools via FIFO input, FITS file I/O, and pipe-based workflows.

docs.title: FIFO Input Mode
docs.text:
The CLI can receive commands from a named pipe (FIFO) in addition to interactive keyboard input. This allows external processes to send commands to a running milk-cli session.

Enabling FIFO mode:

Flag Effect -f / --fifoflag Enable fifo; path auto-generated -F PATH / --fifoname=PATH Enable fifo; use PATH as fifo file

The auto-generated path follows the template:

$SHMDIR/.<processname>.fifo.<PID>

For example, with default settings and PID 12345:

/dev/shm/.1740801234p12345.fifo.0012345

Use -n NAME together with -f to produce a friendlier path:

$ milk-cli -n myctl -f   # /dev/shm/.myctl.fifo.<PID>

Sending commands to a running session:

From a separate shell, write newline-terminated commands to the fifo:

$ echo "mem.listim" > /dev/shm/.myctl.fifo.0012345

The CLI processes one line per select iteration and returns to interactive input once the pipe is drained.

Startup script via fifo:

Use -s FILE together with -f or -F to pre-load a startup script. The file content is piped into the fifo before accepting interactive input:

$ milk-cli -n myctl -F /tmp/myfifo -s setup.milk

docs.title: FITS File I/O
docs.text:
FITSIO is used for FITS file I/O. Requires USE_CFITSIO=ON. See Build Tiers.

milk-cli > iofits.loadfits im1.fits imf1       # load as "imf1"
milk-cli > iofits.loadfits im1.fits            # auto-name from filename
milk-cli > iofits.loadfits im1.fits.gz im1     # load compressed FITS
milk-cli > iofits.save_fl im1 imf1.fits        # save as float
milk-cli > iofits.save_fl im1 "!im1.fits"      # overwrite existing file

docs.title: Driving milk-cli via FIFO
docs.text:
Start milk-cli with the -f flag to enable FIFO input (see FIFO Input Mode). External processes can then send commands through the named pipe.

From inside milk-cli (assuming FIFO is at /dev/shm/.myctl.fifo.<PID>):

milk-cli > !ls im*.fits | xargs -I {} echo iofits.loadfits {} > /dev/shm/.myctl.fifo.0012345

From a separate shell (while milk-cli -n myctl -f is running):

$ ls im*.fits | xargs -I {} echo iofits.loadfits {} > /dev/shm/.myctl.fifo.0012345

docs.title: Using imlist.txt
docs.text:
Start milk-cli with -l (or --listimf) to maintain imlist.txt — an ASCII table of all images currently in memory. Standard Unix tools can filter this list and generate commands.

The -l flag works independently of FIFO mode. You can feed the generated commands back into the CLI via cmdfile.txt or via a FIFO:

Via cmdfile.txt (no -f flag needed):

milk-cli > !awk '{if ($4>200) print $2}' imlist.txt \
        | xargs -I {} echo iofits.save_fl {} {}_tmp.fits > cmdfile.txt

Via FIFO (requires -f or -F; start with milk-cli -l -n myctl -f):

milk-cli > !awk '{if ($4>200) print $2}' imlist.txt \
        | xargs -I {} echo iofits.save_fl {} {}_tmp.fits > /dev/shm/.myctl.fifo.0012345

← Documentation Index

docs.title: Readline Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text:
The milk CLI uses the GNU Readline library for line editing. This page lists the most useful keybindings.

Tip

For the complete reference, see the official Readline User Manual.

See also: CLI Overview · CLI Syntax · Scripting

docs.title: Notation
docs.text: Prefix Meaning C-x Hold Ctrl and press x M-x Hold Alt/Meta and press x (or press Esc then x)

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Key Action C-a Move to start of line C-e Move to end of line M-f Move forward one word M-b Move backward one word C-l Clear screen, reprint current line

docs.title: Editing
docs.text: Key Action C-_ / C-x C-u Undo last edit C-t Transpose characters M-t Transpose words M-u Uppercase current word M-l Lowercase current word M-c Capitalize current word

docs.title: Kill & Yank (Cut & Paste)
docs.text: Key Action C-k Kill from cursor to end of line C-w Kill previous word (whitespace-delimited) M-d Kill from cursor to end of word M-DEL Kill from cursor to start of word C-y Yank (paste) most recently killed text M-y Rotate kill-ring after C-y

docs.title: History
docs.text: Key Action ↑ / C-p Previous history entry ↓ / C-n Next history entry C-r Reverse incremental search M-< Jump to first history entry M-> Jump to last (current) entry

docs.title: Completion
docs.text:
Key Action TAB Autocomplete (commands, filenames) M-? List possible completions M-* Insert all completions

← CLI Overview · Documentation Index

docs.title: Scripting
docs.text:
The milk-cli shell supports bash-like scripting constructs: variables, arithmetic, flow control, user-defined functions, and script files. This page documents the full scripting system.

See also: CLI Syntax · FPS · Streams

docs.title: Variables
docs.text: Click to expand

docs.title: Setting and Reading
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
x=42
name=hello
echo $x          # prints: 42
echo ${name}     # prints: hello

Variable names are case-sensitive and may contain letters, digits, and underscores. No spaces around =.

docs.title: Listing and Removing
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
vars              # list all variables
unset x           # remove variable x

docs.title: Special Variables
docs.text: Variable Description $? Exit status of last command (0=success) $HOME, $PATH, … Environment variables

docs.title: String Operations
docs.text:
The ${...} expansion supports bash-like string manipulation:

Syntax Description ${#var} String length ${var:offset:length} Substring extraction ${var%%pattern} Strip longest suffix match ${var##pattern} Strip longest prefix match ${var^^} Uppercase all characters ${var,,} Lowercase all characters ${var^} Capitalize first character ${var,} Lowercase first character 
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
path=/home/user/file.txt
echo ${#path}           # prints: 19
echo ${path:6:4}        # prints: user
echo ${path%%/*}        # prints: (empty)
echo ${path##*/}        # prints: file.txt
name=hello
echo ${name^^}          # prints: HELLO
name=WORLD
echo ${name,,}          # prints: world

docs.title: Array Variables
docs.text:
Arrays store multiple values indexed by integer:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
colors=(red green blue)
echo ${colors[0]}       # prints: red
echo ${colors[2]}       # prints: blue
echo ${colors[@]}       # prints: red green blue
echo ${#colors[@]}      # prints: 3

docs.title: FPS Parameter Access
docs.text:
Read FPS parameters using @fpsname.param syntax:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
echo @myloop.loopgain      # read FPS param
g=@myloop.loopgain         # store in variable

Write FPS parameters with fpsset:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
fpsset myloop loopgain 0.5

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text:
Click to expand

$(( expr )) evaluates integer arithmetic with +, -, *, /, % operators. Variables and FPS parameters are expanded inside the expression:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
x=10
y=$(( x + 5 ))        # y = 15
z=$(( y * 2 - x ))    # z = 20
echo $y $z            # prints: 15 20

docs.title: Built-in Commands
docs.text: Click to expand

docs.title: sleep
docs.text:
Pause execution for a given number of seconds (float-capable):

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
sleep 1.5             # pause 1.5 seconds
sleep 0.01            # 10 ms pause

docs.title: printf
docs.text:
Formatted output supporting %s, %d, %f, %%, and \n, \t escape sequences:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
printf "value = %d\n" 42
printf "%s has %d items\n" list 5

docs.title: read
docs.text:
Read a line from standard input into a variable:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
read name
hello world
echo $name         # prints: hello world

Flags:

Flag Description -p "prompt" Display a prompt before reading -t N Timeout after N seconds -a arrayname Split words into an array 
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
read -p "Enter value: " val
Enter value: 42
echo $val           # prints: 42
read -t 5 response  # wait up to 5 sec
read -a words       # split into array
hello world
echo ${words[0]}    # prints: hello

docs.title: Logical Operators
docs.text:
Chain commands with && (AND) and || (OR):

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
cmd1 && cmd2        # cmd2 runs if cmd1 succeeds
cmd1 || cmd2        # cmd2 runs if cmd1 fails

docs.title: Brace Expansion
docs.text:
Expand {N..M} and {N..M..S} into integer sequences:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
echo {1..5}         # prints: 1 2 3 4 5
echo {0..10..2}     # prints: 0 2 4 6 8 10
echo {5..1}         # prints: 5 4 3 2 1

Useful with for loops:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
for i in {1..5}; do
    echo item $i
done

docs.title: Pipes
docs.text:
Pipe the output of one command into another:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
echo hello | read greeting
listim | grep wfs

docs.title: Output Redirection
docs.text:
Redirect stdout to a file:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
echo "log entry" > output.txt
echo "more" >> output.txt  # append

docs.title: Stderr Redirection
docs.text:
Redirect stderr independently:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
cmd 2>&1          # stderr to stdout
cmd 2>/dev/null    # discard stderr
cmd 2>errors.txt   # stderr to file

docs.title: Here-Strings
docs.text:
Provide a string as stdin to a command:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
read name <<< "world"
echo $name            # prints: world

docs.title: Glob Expansion
docs.text:
Tokens containing * or ? are expanded to matching filenames:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
echo *.fits           # all FITS files
echo data_??.bin      # data_01.bin etc.

Quoted globs are not expanded: echo "*.fits" prints the literal *.fits.

docs.title: exit
docs.text:
Exit the CLI session with an optional status code:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
exit          # exit with status 0
exit 1        # exit with status 1

docs.title: shift
docs.text:
Shift positional parameters ($1→$2, etc.) inside functions:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
function process_all {
    while [ -n "$1" ]; do
        echo processing $1
        shift
    done
}
process_all a b c

docs.title: trap
docs.text:
Register signal handlers that execute a command when a signal is received:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
trap 'echo cleanup' EXIT
trap 'rm /tmp/lockfile' INT TERM

Supported signals: EXIT, INT, TERM, HUP, USR1, USR2, or numeric.

docs.title: set
docs.text:
Control shell behavior flags:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
set -e      # exit on error
set -x      # trace commands (+ prefix)
set +e      # disable -e
set +x      # disable -x
set -ex     # enable both

docs.title: export
docs.text:
Set environment variables visible to child processes:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
export DMSHMDIR="/tmp/shm"
export VERBOSE=1
export PATH              # push current $PATH

docs.title: Extended Test [[ ]]
docs.text:
Extended conditional test with regex support:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
[[ $filename =~ ^data_[0-9]+$ ]]
[[ -n $myvar ]]
[[ -f $path ]]

docs.title: Tilde Expansion
docs.text:
~ expands to $HOME at the start of tokens:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
echo ~/data          # /home/user/data
ls ~/scripts/*.sh

docs.title: Input Redirection
docs.text:
Read a file as standard input:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
read line < config.txt
cmd < input.dat

docs.title: select
docs.text:
Interactive numbered menu loop:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
select mode in fast normal slow; do
    echo "Selected: $mode"
    break
done

docs.title: Arithmetic For
docs.text:
C-style counted loop using for ((;;)):

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
for ((i=0; i<5; i++)); do
    echo "iteration $i"
done

docs.title: Parameter Defaults
docs.text:
Use ${var:-default} to substitute a default value when a variable is unset or empty:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
echo ${name:-anonymous}
echo ${dir:=/tmp}
echo ${v:+yes}
echo ${v:?error message}
Syntax Meaning ${v:-def} Expand to def if unset ${v:=def} Assign def if unset ${v:+alt} Expand to alt if set ${v:?err} Error message if unset

docs.title: String Operations
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
path="/home/user/file.txt"
echo ${path/user/admin}
echo ${path//\//|}
echo ${path#/home/}
echo ${path%.txt}
Syntax Meaning ${v/pat/rep} Replace first match ${v//pat/rep} Replace all matches ${v#pat} Strip shortest prefix ${v%pat} Strip shortest suffix

docs.title: Source (Include Files)
docs.text:
Execute commands from a file in the current environment:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
source config.sh
. config.sh

docs.title: Read-Only Variables
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
readonly PI=3.14159

docs.title: Break / Continue with Count
docs.text:
Exit or skip multiple loop levels:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
for i in 1 2 3; do
    for j in a b c; do
        break 2
    done
done

docs.title: Printf
docs.text:
Format output with %s, %d, %f specifiers:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
printf "Name: %s Age: %d\n" Alice 30
printf "PI = %f\n" 3.14159

docs.title: Getopts
docs.text:
Parse command-line options:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
OPTIND=1
while getopts "vf:" opt; do
    echo "opt=$opt OPTARG=$OPTARG"
done

docs.title: Mapfile / Readarray
docs.text:
Read lines from a file into an array:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
mapfile -t lines < input.txt
echo ${lines[0]}
echo ${#lines[@]}

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text:
Run commands in the background and wait:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
long_command &
echo "PID is $!"
wait

docs.title: Subshell Grouping
docs.text:
Execute commands in an isolated sub-environment:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
(x=42; echo $x)
echo $x    # empty — subshell is isolated

docs.title: declare / typeset
docs.text:
Declare variable attributes:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
declare -i count=0    # integer
declare -r PI=3.14    # read-only
declare -a arr        # array
declare -x MYVAR=val  # export
typeset -i x=5        # alias
Flag Meaning -i Integer variable -a Array variable -r Read-only -x Export to environment

docs.title: let
docs.text:
Evaluate arithmetic expressions:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
let "x=5+3"       # x = 8
let "y=x*2"       # y = 16
let "x++"         # x = 9

docs.title: eval
docs.text:
Construct and execute a command string:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
cmd="echo hello"
eval $cmd          # prints: hello
vname=foo
eval "$vname=42"
echo $foo           # prints: 42

docs.title: type / command -v
docs.text:
Check whether a command exists:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
type echo           # echo is a builtin
command -v ls        # /usr/bin/ls
type nonexistent     # not found

docs.title: timeout
docs.text:
Run a command with a deadline:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
timeout 5 long_running_cmd

If the command does not finish within N seconds, it is terminated with $? set to 124.

docs.title: Flow Control
docs.text: Click to expand

docs.title: if / elif / else / fi
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
x=10
if [ $x -gt 100 ]; then
    echo big
elif [ $x -gt 5 ]; then
    echo medium
else
    echo small
fi
# prints: medium

elif branches are evaluated in order. The first matching condition executes its body.

The [ ... ] syntax supports these test operators:

Operator Meaning -eq equal -ne not equal -gt greater than -ge greater or equal -lt less than -le less or equal = string equal != string not equal -n str string is non-empty -z str string is empty -f path regular file exists -d path directory exists -e path path exists (any type) -s path file exists and is non-empty ! expr logical NOT (negate result)

docs.title: while / do / done
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
n=1
while [ $n -le 5 ]; do
    echo iteration $n
    n=$(( n + 1 ))
done

Use break to exit early, continue to skip to the next iteration:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
n=0
while [ $n -lt 10 ]; do
    n=$(( n + 1 ))
    if [ $n -eq 3 ]; then
        continue
    fi
    if [ $n -eq 7 ]; then
        break
    fi
    echo $n
done

docs.title: for / do / done
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
for item in alpha beta gamma; do
    echo processing $item
done

docs.title: Nesting
docs.text:
All flow control constructs can be nested:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
n=0
while [ $n -lt 3 ]; do
    n=$(( n + 1 ))
    if [ $n -eq 2 ]; then
        echo found two
    fi
    echo n=$n
done

docs.title: case / esac
docs.text:
Multi-way branching by pattern matching:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
mode=fast
case $mode in
  fast) echo speed ;;
  safe|careful) echo caution ;;
  *) echo unknown ;;
esac
# prints: speed

Patterns support | alternation and * wildcard. Only the first matching pattern's body is executed.

docs.title: Functions
Return Values
docs.text:
Use return to exit a function early. An optional integer argument sets $?:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
function check {
    if [ $1 -gt 10 ]; then
        return 0
    fi
    return 1
}
check 20
echo $?               # prints: 0

docs.title: Local Variable Scoping
docs.text:
By default, variables assigned within a function are global. Use the local keyword to explicitly bound a variable to the function's scope. The local keyword safely shadows any existing global variables, restoring them when returning.

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
x=global
y=global
function test {
    x=modified
    local y=localized
}
test
echo $x               # prints: modified
echo $y               # prints: global

docs.title: Heredocs
docs.text:
Click to expand

Assign multi-line text to a variable using heredoc syntax:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
config=<<EOF
gain=0.5
nframes=100
mode=closed
EOF
echo $config

Lines between =<<DELIM and DELIM are concatenated with newlines and stored in the variable.

docs.title: Stream Event Triggers
Script Files
docs.text: Click to expand

docs.title: Running Scripts
docs.text:
Use source (or the shorthand .) to execute a script file:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
source myscript.milk
. myscript.milk        # same thing

Blank lines and # comments are skipped. On error, the filename and line number are printed.

docs.title: Include Guard
docs.text:
include_once sources a file only once per session, even if called multiple times. Uses resolved paths:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
include_once helpers.milk
include_once helpers.milk   # no-op

docs.title: Startup Profile
docs.text: ~/.milkrc is automatically sourced at startup if it exists. Use this for persistent aliases, variables, and function definitions.

docs.title: Saving State
docs.text:
Export all current variables and function definitions to a file:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
savescript state.milk

The saved file can be loaded later with source.

docs.title: Saving History
docs.text:
Write the readline command history to a file:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
savehistory replay.milk

This creates a script that replays your interactive session.

docs.title: Example Script
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
# setup.milk — initialize processing pipeline

# Configuration
nframes=100
gain=0.5

# Create shared memory images
mem.mk2Dim wfs 128 128
mem.mk2Dim dm 32 32

# Define a helper function
function run_loop {
    n=0
    while [ $n -lt $nframes ]; do
        n=$(( n + 1 ))
        echo frame $n
    done
}

# Execute
run_loop
echo "Processing complete"

docs.text: Feature Detail Extension .milk (by convention) Comments Lines starting with # Shebang #!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s Startup -s FILE flag on command line Auto-load ~/.milkrc at startup

docs.title: Associative Arrays
docs.text:
Click to expand

Associative arrays store key-value pairs:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
declare -A config
config[host]=localhost
config[port]=8080
echo ${config[host]}   # localhost

Assignment uses map[key]=value syntax. Lookup uses ${map[key]} expansion.

docs.title: Indirect Expansion
docs.text:
Click to expand

${!var} expands to the value of the variable whose name is stored in var:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
target=myval
myval=42
echo ${!target}   # 42

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Click to expand 
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
alias ll='listim'
alias s='readshmim'
ll                    # runs: listim
alias                 # list all aliases
unalias ll            # remove alias

Aliases are expanded before command dispatch.

docs.title: Path Utilities
docs.text:
Click to expand 
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
basename /data/img.fits   # img.fits
dirname /data/img.fits    # /data

docs.title: Directory Stack
docs.text:
Click to expand 
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
pushd /data           # cd to /data
pushd /tmp            # cd to /tmp
dirs                  # show stack
popd                  # back to /data
popd                  # back to original

docs.title: Number Sequences
docs.text:
Click to expand 
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
seq 5                 # 1 2 3 4 5
seq 2 5               # 2 3 4 5
seq 0 0.1 1.0         # 0 0.1 ... 1.0
seq 10 -2 0           # 10 8 6 4 2 0

Supports floating-point steps.

docs.title: Builtins
docs.text:
Click to expand 
#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
true                  # $? = 0
false                 # $? = 1
if (( x > 5 )); then echo big; fi

docs.title: Variable Testing
docs.text:
Click to expand

test -v VAR checks if a variable is set:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
x=1
if [ -v x ]; then echo set; fi

docs.title: Stream & FPS Metadata
docs.text:
Click to expand

Access shared memory stream properties via dot-syntax variable expansion:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
echo ${mystream.xsize}   # X dimension
echo ${mystream.ysize}   # Y dimension
echo ${mystream.zsize}   # Z dimension
echo ${mystream.type}    # datatype code
echo ${mystream.cnt0}    # frame counter
echo ${mystream.naxis}   # number of axes

FPS status can be checked:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
echo ${myfps.status}     # 1 if exists

docs.title: Wait for Resources
docs.text:
Click to expand

Wait for shared memory streams or FPS to appear:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
waitfor_stream wfs 30    # wait up to 30s
waitfor_fps dmcomb 10    # wait up to 10s

Returns 0 on success, 1 on timeout. Default timeout: 10 seconds.

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
# Pattern: wait for stream, then process
waitfor_stream wfs 60
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Stream ready: ${wfs.xsize}x${wfs.ysize}"
fi

docs.title: Scripting Showcase
docs.text:
Click to expand

Here are examples demonstrating the combined capabilities of milk-cli's built-in scripting engine, ordered from simple to complex.

← CLI Syntax · Documentation Index

docs.title: Simple
docs.text:
Example 1: Hello World and Variables

The simplest possible script — setting variables and printing them:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
name=world
echo "Hello, ${name}!"
x=42
echo "The answer is $x"

Expected output:

Hello, world!
The answer is 42
Example 2: Arithmetic and String Length

Use $(( )) for integer arithmetic and ${#var} for string length:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
a=8
b=3
echo "Sum:     $(( a + b ))"
echo "Product: $(( a * b ))"
echo "Division: $(( a / b ))"
echo "Modulo:  $(( a % b ))"

word=spectral
echo "Length of '${word}': ${#word}"

Expected output:

Sum:     11
Product: 24
Division: 2
Modulo:  2
Length of 'spectral': 8
Example 3: Conditional Logic

Branch on exit status or integer comparisons:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
temp=72

if [ $temp -lt 60 ]; then
    echo "Cold"
elif [ $temp -lt 80 ]; then
    echo "Comfortable"
else
    echo "Hot"
fi

Expected output:

Comfortable
Example 4: Looping Over a Range

for loops over sequences with seq, or literal lists:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
# Loop over a numeric sequence
for i in $(seq 1 5); do
    echo "Frame $i"
done

# Loop over a literal list
for color in red green blue; do
    echo "Channel: $color"
done

Expected output:

Frame 1
Frame 2
Frame 3
Frame 4
Frame 5
Channel: red
Channel: green
Channel: blue

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
Example 5: Parameter Defaults and String Manipulation

Safely provide defaults for arguments and cleanly parse paths:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
function process_image {
    local img_path=${1:-/data/default.fits}
    local filename=${img_path##*/}   # strip path prefix
    local basename=${filename%.*}    # strip extension

    echo "Processing ${basename}..."
}

process_image
process_image /tmp/test_image.fits

Expected output:

Processing default...
Processing test_image...
Example 6: Functions and Return Values

Functions use return to pass integer exit status back to $?. Use command substitution $(...) to capture printed output:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
function clamp {
    local val=$1 lo=$2 hi=$3
    if [ $val -lt $lo ]; then
        echo $lo
    elif [ $val -gt $hi ]; then
        echo $hi
    else
        echo $val
    fi
}

result=$(clamp 150 0 100)
echo "Clamped: $result"

result=$(clamp -5 0 100)
echo "Clamped: $result"

Expected output:

Clamped: 100
Clamped: 0
Example 7: Arrays and Iteration

Build an array and iterate over its elements:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
streams=(wfs_cam dm_disp tt_disp)

echo "Registered streams: ${#streams[@]}"

for i in $(seq 0 $(( ${#streams[@]} - 1 ))); do
    echo "  [$i] ${streams[$i]}"
done

Expected output:

Registered streams: 3
  [0] wfs_cam
  [1] dm_disp
  [2] tt_disp
Example 8: While Loop and Counter

Accumulate a running sum with a while loop:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
total=0
count=0
max=10

while [ $count -lt $max ]; do
    total=$(( total + count ))
    count=$(( count + 1 ))
done

echo "Sum 0..$(( max - 1 )) = $total"

Expected output:

Sum 0..9 = 45
Example 9: Local Variables and Recursion

Use local variables and return to safely write recursive functions:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
function factorial {
    local n=$1
    if [ $n -le 1 ]; then
        return 1
    else
        local prev=$(( n - 1 ))
        factorial $prev
        return $(( n * $? ))
    fi
}

factorial 5
echo "5! = $?"

Expected output:

5! = 120
Example 10: Transparent OS Fallback and Command Substitution

Combine Linux shell utilities with native milk-cli variables without the ! prefix required for interactive mode:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
prefix="output_"
ext=".fits"

# Count FITS files in the current directory
count=$(ls -1 | grep -c "${ext}")
echo "Found $count FITS files."

# Timestamp tag for unique filenames
tag=$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)
echo "Saving to: ${prefix}${tag}${ext}"

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
Example 11: Waiting for Streams

Block until shared-memory streams become available, then read their geometry via dot-expansion:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
function wait_and_monitor {
    local stream=$1
    echo "Waiting for stream ${stream}..."

    waitfor_stream $stream 60
    if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
        echo "Error: Stream ${stream} timed out."
        return 1
    fi

    # Read stream metadata via dot-expansion
    echo "Ready! Shape: ${${stream}.xsize}x${${stream}.ysize}"
}

wait_and_monitor wfs_cam
wait_and_monitor dm_disp
Example 12: FPS Parameter Manipulation

Read and write FPS parameters from a script to automate configuration changes across multiple compute units:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
# Set loop gain on the DM combiner FPS
milk-fps-set dmcomb.loopgain 0.05

# Retrieve current value and log it
gain=$(milk-fps-set dmcomb.loopgain)
echo "DM combiner gain set to: $gain"

# Apply identical gain to all modal channels
nmodes=50
for m in $(seq 0 $(( nmodes - 1 ))); do
    milk-fps-set dmcomb.modesgain[$m] 0.1
done

echo "Set $nmodes modal gains to 0.1"
Example 13: Stream Diagnostic Report

Collect live metadata from multiple streams and format a compact diagnostic table:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s
streams=(wfs_cam dm_disp wfs_ref)

echo "--------------------------------------------"
echo "  Stream           XSize  YSize  Frame"
echo "--------------------------------------------"

for s in ${streams[@]}; do
    waitfor_stream $s 5
    if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
        printf "  %-18s OFFLINE\n" $s
        continue
    fi

    xs=${${s}.xsize}
    ys=${${s}.ysize}
    cnt=${${s}.cnt0}
    printf "  %-18s %-6s %-6s %s\n" $s $xs $ys $cnt
done

echo "--------------------------------------------"
Example 14: AO Loop Startup Orchestration

A complete startup script that initialises an AO loop step by step, verifies each stage, and aborts cleanly on failure:

#!/usr/bin/env milk-cli -s

# ---------- helpers ----------
function die {
    echo "FATAL: $1"
    exit 1
}

function wait_stream {
    local s=$1 timeout=${2:-30}
    waitfor_stream $s $timeout
    [ $? -ne 0 ] && die "Stream '$s' not available after ${timeout}s"
    echo "  [OK] $s  ${${s}.xsize}x${${s}.ysize}"
}

# ---------- 1. verify hardware streams ----------
echo "=== 1. Checking hardware streams ==="
wait_stream wfs_cam 60
wait_stream dm_volt

# ---------- 2. load reference PSF ----------
echo "=== 2. Loading WFS reference ==="
milk-FITS2shm wfs_ref.fits wfs_ref
wait_stream wfs_ref

# ---------- 3. start modal decomposition FPS ----------
echo "=== 3. Starting modal decomposition ==="
milk-fpsexec-cacaoloop-WFS -n wfs01 -tmux
sleep 2
waitfor_stream wfs_modes 20
[ $? -ne 0 ] && die "Modal decomposition failed to produce wfs_modes"

# ---------- 4. configure loop gains ----------
echo "=== 4. Configuring loop gains ==="
nmodes=100
for m in $(seq 0 $(( nmodes - 1 ))); do
    milk-fps-set dmcomb.modesgain[$m] 0.05
done
milk-fps-set dmcomb.loopgain 1.0
milk-fps-set dmcomb.loopON 1

# ---------- 5. confirm loop is running ----------
echo "=== 5. Loop status ==="
sleep 1
fpsgain=$(milk-fps-set dmcomb.loopgain)
echo "  loopgain = $fpsgain"
echo "AO loop started successfully."

This document outlines the conventions for documenting the milk project. The documentation is split into two halves:

docs.title: 1. Writing Manuals and Guides (Markdown)
docs.text:
General instructional documentation, architectural overviews, and tutorials should be placed in the docs/ folder in standard GitHub Flavored Markdown (.md).

  • Use MkDocs admonitions (!!! note, !!! warning, !!! tip) to call out important information. Indent the body by four spaces.
  • Use Markdown tables for data and parameter lists.
  • When referencing other files, use standard relative markdown links (e.g., [Coding Standards](coding_standards.md)).

docs.title: 2. Documenting Source Code (Doxygen)
docs.text:
The milk C/C++ source code uses Doxygen tags to generate the API reference.

Doxygen comments should be placed directly above the function implementations in the .c files, or above the struct definitions in the .h files.

docs.title: 2.1 Standard Function Documentation
docs.text:
Use the standard @param, @return, and @brief tags to describe the function behavior.

/**
 * @ingroup processing_module
 * @brief Computes the sum of two integers.
 *
 * Detailed description of the computation can go here. 
 * You can also include formulas or extended methodology.
 *
 * @param[in]  a first number
 * @param[in]  b second number to be added to first one
 * @param[out] output string buffer where the result is written
 *
 * @return error code, #RETURN_SUCCESS if OK
 */
inline static errno_t compute_sum(int a, int b, char *output) {
    int sum = a + b;
    sprintf(output, "%d", sum);
    return RETURN_SUCCESS;
}

docs.title: 2.2 Grouping Modules
docs.text:
Use @defgroup and @ingroup to group related functions into unified modules in the generated HTML reference.

/**
 * @defgroup FPSconf Configuration function for Function Parameter Structure (FPS)
 * @defgroup FPSrun  Run function using Function Parameter Structure (FPS)
 */

docs.title: 3. Building the Doxygen HTML Reference
docs.text: If you wish to view the generated C API documentation locally, you can build it using Doxygen.

docs.title: 3.1 Initial Requirements
docs.text:
Ensure you have Doxygen installed on your system:

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install doxygen graphviz

# CentOS/RHEL
sudo yum install doxygen graphviz

docs.title: 3.2 Generating the Documentation
docs.text:
A tracked Doxyfile is maintained at the repository root. It is also used by CI (.github/workflows/docs.yml) to deploy the API reference to GitHub Pages on every push to main or framework-dev.

To generate the documentation locally:

  1. Navigate to the repository root.
  2. Run Doxygen:
doxygen Doxyfile
  1. Open the generated output:
xdg-open docs/doxygen/html/index.html

Tip

The CI workflow automatically deploys to GitHub Pages. Check the repository's Pages settings for the live URL.

docs.title: Loading, Creating Additional Modules
docs.text:
Note

This file: docs/developer/LoadingModules.md

Users can create additional modules, and following a few milk-specific conventions, link their functions to the milk CLI. Additional modules can be added to the existing build process or compiled separately and then loaded at runtime.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text: milk is oganized in modules, each compiled as a shared object and loaded at runtime.

docs.title: 1.1. Compiling
docs.text:
While milk comes with its own set of modules, others can be added at runtime. Modules that conform to milk specifications can be downloaded and added by following these steps:

# execute these commands from the source root directory (for example ~./milk/)
# move to source subdir, where module directories are located
$ cd ./src

# Download a new module
$ git clone https://github.com/milk-org/NewModuleName

# move to build directory
$ cd ../_build

# Add new module to compile script
$ cmake .. -DEXTRAMODULES="NewModuleName"

# compile and install
$ sudo make install

docs.title: 1.2. Runtime linking
docs.text:
Note that the commands above will compile the module into a shared object, but it will not be loaded by default at runtime. There are 4 options to load the module into the milk executable, detailed in the following section. For example, the new module may be loaded within the milk command line interface as follows:

# start milk
$ milk-cli

# load module from command line interface
milk-cli > mload NewModuleName

# check list of modules. NewModuleName should appear
milk-cli > m?

docs.title: 1.3. A simple example
docs.text:
milk includes an example module, which is not compiled or linked by default, to demonstrate how to write and add modules.

The example module is in directory src/milk_module_example :

$ cd src/milk_module_example
$ ls
CMakeLists.txt
examplefunc1.c
examplefunc1.h
examplefunc2_FPS.c
examplefunc2_FPS.h
examplefunc4_streamprocess.c
examplefunc4_streamprocess.h
examplefunc_fps_cli_poc.c    # V2 template
milk_module_example.c
milk_module_example.h

Check the source code (well documented) to see how modules are written. To compile :

$ cd _build
$ cmake .. -DEXTRAMODULES="milk_module_example"
$ sudo make install

Lets run it :

# start milk
$ milk-cli

# load module as "mex" (short for module example)
milk-cli > mloadas milk_module_example mex

# check we have it
milk-cli > m?

# run the test function, which creates an image
# note you can tab complete after typying "mex." to list functions
milk-cli > mex.func1 im1 1.2

# check the image is in memory
milk-cli > mem.listim

docs.title: 2.1. Automatic linking from ./lib/ directory
docs.text: Any shared object in the ./lib/ subdirectory of source code will be loaded upon startup.

docs.title: 2.2. Linking module from within CLI with soload
docs.text:
Pre-compiled modules can be linked with the soload command within the CLI:

milk-cli > soload <fullsoname>

The fullsoname is the shared object file name, path relative to current directory. For example "../mylib/myodule.so".

Provided that the module follows milk conventions, linking the module will add the corresponding functions to the CLI. This can be checked by probing the module functions:

milk-cli > m?                # lists linked modules
milk-cli > m? <modulename>   # lists CLI commands in the module

docs.title: 2.3. Linking module from within CLI with mload
docs.text:
By default, modules shared objects are installed in /usr/local/lib, and are named lib<ModuleName>.so. With these assumptions satisfied, modules can be linked from within the CLI with the mload command:

milk-cli > mload <modulename>

Alternatively, a short name can be specified

milk-cli > mloadas <modulename> <shortname>

Module functions are called from the command line interface prompt:

milk-cli > <shortname>.<functionname> <arguments...>

docs.title: 2.4. Using environment variable CLI_ADD_LIBS to link shared objects
docs.text:
Upon startup, milk will read the CLI_ADD_LIBS environment variable to link shared objects. For example:

CLI_ADD_LIBS="/usr/local/libs/libMyFirstModule.so /usr/local/libs/libMySecondModule.so" milk-cli

will link modules MyFirstModule and MySecondModule.

Note

Shared object names can be separated by space, semicolon, or comma.

docs.title: 3.1. Principles
docs.text:
Modules that are always loaded upon startup are registered in the module's initlib_<modulename> function, which is called automatically when the shared object is loaded. Additional modules may be loaded using the C dlopen() command. The library should include a function initlib_<modulename> to be executed when the module is loaded. This function should register functions to the command line interface, as done for all other modules that are part of the distribution.

\see http://www.linux-mag.com/id/1028/ for instructions to create shared libraries that can be loaded as modules. \see https://www.gnu.org/software/automake/manual/html_node/Libtool-Convenience-Libraries.html

docs.title: 3.2. Adding modules to the main package compilation
docs.text:
The preferred way to add modules is to have them within the main source code directory alongside default modules, following the same conventions and locations as the default modules. A new module should then have the following files in the ./src/<ModuleName>/ directory:

  • CMakeLists.txt file
  • source code files (.c and .h files)

The EXTRAMODULES option is then used to add entry(ies) to the list of compiled modules. For example:

cmake .. -DEXTRAMODULES="WFpropagate;OpticsMaterials"

will compile modules WFpropagate and OpticsMaterials in addition to default modules. The extra modules shared objects will be /usr/local/lib/libWFpropagate.so and /usr/local/lib/libOpticsMaterials.so, and can be loaded with any of the methods described in the linking section.

Warning

Adding entries with the EXTRAMODULES option will compile the corresponding shared objects, but will not have them loaded upon execution of the main executable by default. See section below on Automatic loading.

docs.title: 3.3. Automatic loading
docs.text:
Several options are available to have the additional module(s) automatically loaded every time:

  • Copy or link the shared object to the ./lib/ directory.

For example:

ln -s /usr/local/lib/libWFpropagate.so ~/src/milk/lib/libWFpropagate.so
  • Create a system-wide environment variable CLI_ADD_LIBS in ~/.bashrc.

Note

Several versions of the executable can also be defined, each with its own set of automatically loaded modules. For example, the following line can be saved as an executable script:

CLI_ADD_LIBS="/usr/local/libs/libWFpropagate.so" milk-cli

docs.title: 3.4. Adding new module to github
docs.text:
We assume here that you have created a module and you would like to push it to the main github package org (we assume here milk-org).

# First, create the repo in github, then run the following commands:
cd ./MyModuleName/
git init
git add .
git commit -m "First commit"
git remote add origin https://github.com/milk-org/MyModuleName
git config credential.helper store       # For convenience
git push --set-upstream origin main
# Now we create framework-dev branch
git checkout -b framework-dev
git push --set-upstream origin framework-dev

docs.title: 4. Custom modules
docs.text:
Additional custom modules may also be compiled independently from the main compile process. This is not the preferred option, and there is a performance hit, as the benefits of link-time optimization will be lost.

To compile a custom module :

cd exampleModule
gcc -c -I.. -fPIC exampleModule.c
gcc -c -fPIC compute_pi.c -Ofast
gcc -shared -I.. -fPIC exampleModule.o compute_pi.o -o libexamplemodule.so -lc

To load the new modules automatically on milk startup, create a sym link in the milk's lib directory:

cd ~/src/milk/lib
ln -s ../src/exampleModule/libexamplemodule.so libexamplemodule.so

Alternatively, you can load it from the CLI at anytime:

milk-cli > soload "<pathtomilk>/src/exampleModule/libexamplemodule.so"

docs.title: Module Files
docs.text:
The code is organized in modules under two main directories:

See also: Programmer's Guide · Coding Standards · Adding Plugins · Template Source Code

Location Contains src/ Core modules (engine, CLI, coremods) plugins/ Optional plugin modules

Within each module directory:

Path Content <modulename>.c Main C source and module registration <modulename>.h Module header and function prototypes CMakeLists.txt CMake build configuration README.md Module overview, source file list, dependencies scripts/ Shell scripts and utilities (optional) *.c / *.h Additional source files for individual functions

Modules are compiled into shared object libraries (.so) and loaded by milk-cli at runtime. Standalone executables (milk-fpsexec-*) are built separately and installed to bin/.

docs.title: Working with git
docs.text:
Note

This file: docs/developer/WorkingWithGit.md

See also: Documenting Code · Adding Plugins · Compile Instructions

docs.title: 1. Source Code and Modules
docs.text:
Most of milk's code is organized in directories under src/ (core modules) and plugins/ (optional modules). Modules are compiled as shared objects loaded by the main process at runtime.

Some plugin directories (e.g., plugins/cacao-src) may be symbolic links to external source trees or git submodules.

docs.title: 2. Standard Development Workflow
docs.text:
All code changes must go through a pull request. Never commit directly to framework-dev (or main).

CRITICAL BRANCHING RULE:

  • You are STRICTLY FORBIDDEN from modifying or pushing to the dev branch for milk, cacao, and ImageStreamIO.
  • You must ONLY push to and merge into framework-dev or feature branches derived from framework-dev.

docs.title: Required Steps
docs.text:
1. Create a feature branch from framework-dev:

  2. Use a descriptive name, e.g., feat/new-stream-processor, fix/imfunctions-else-if, perf/mvm-blas-upgrade, docs/update-guide.

  3. Make commits on the feature branch. Keep commits atomic and well-described.

  4. Push the feature branch to origin.
  5. Create a PR targeting framework-dev. Include a clear title and description of the changes.
  6. Do not merge — let the maintainer review and merge.

docs.title: 3. Parallel Development using Git Worktrees
docs.text:
The milk project enforces strict branching rules where all work must occur on feature branches off of framework-dev. If you need to work on multiple tracks simultaneously (e.g., optimizing performance while also updating documentation or fixing a CLI bug), you should use Git Worktrees.

Git worktrees allow you to have multiple isolated working directories that share the exact same underlying local .git repository.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Keep the Main Clone Clean: Keep your primary repository (e.g., ~/src/milk) checked out to framework-dev.

  2. Create Track-Specific Worktrees: Create sibling directories for your parallel tracks.

cd ~/src/milk
git worktree add ../milk-docs -b docs/my-task framework-dev
git worktree add ../milk-cli -b feat/my-cli-task framework-dev

  1. Isolate Builds: Each worktree should have its own dedicated _build directory. This ensures CMake caches and compiled object files do not interfere with each other when you context-switch.

  2. Reusing Worktrees: When you finish a task (e.g., your CLI feature is merged), do not delete the worktree. Reuse it for your next CLI task to preserve your CMake build cache:

cd ~/src/milk-cli
git checkout framework-dev
git pull --ff-only origin framework-dev
git checkout -b feat/my-next-cli-task

Tip

A helper script milk-setup-worktrees is available to automatically scaffold this directory layout and initialize the build directories for you.

docs.title: 4. Releasing a New Version
docs.text:
When releasing a new version from framework-dev (or the equivalent stable branch):

  • Update version number in CMakeLists.txt
  • Update version information in README.md

Merge framework-dev into main, then tag:

$ git checkout main
$ git merge framework-dev
$ git tag -a vX.YY.ZZ -m "milk version X.YY.ZZ"
$ git push origin main --tags

Note

Modules that are shared between packages (e.g., milk and cacao) can have parallel version number histories. Any new version, regardless of which package it is associated with, includes all previous changes.

docs.text:

docs.title: Coding Standards
docs.text:
This document outlines the standard C coding conventions expected for the milk project. Consistent conventions help ensure readability, maintainability, and seamless integration of new code or plugins.

See also: Programmer's Guide · Documenting Code · Template Source Code · Module Files

docs.title: General C Code Style
docs.text:
• Linux Kernel Style: Use the Linux kernel's C coding style as the baseline for indentation and formatting, wherever it doesn't conflict with the rules below.
  • Short Lines: Keep lines short, generally no more than 80 characters.
  • Scope limitation: Use code blocks ({ ... }) to reduce the scope of variables as much as possible.

docs.title: Function Signatures
docs.text:
• Multi-line Prototypes: Function prototypes with arguments should be formatted across multiple lines, with exactly one line per argument. This greatly improves diff readability and annotation.
inline static errno_t example_compute_sum(
    int a,
    int b,
    char *output
)

docs.title: Documentation Rules
docs.text:
• Kernel-Doc Style: Document functions using the standard Kernel-Doc (or Doxygen-compatible) style.
  • .h Files: Briefly document the function's overall purpose in the header file.
  • .c Files: Document the purpose and overall approach of the function above the function code in the source file, and detail the methodology within the function itself.

docs.title: Compilation and Headers
docs.text:
• Compiler Warnings: Enable and enforce compiler warnings (-Wall, -Wextra) during development to catch missing declarations early. Treat them as errors (-Werror) in CI/CD pipelines.
  • Explicit Includes: Make sure every .c file strictly includes the exact headers it relies on. Do not implicitly rely on another header to include them (e.g., relying on CLIcore.h to provide <math.h> or <stdlib.h>).

docs.title: Adding a Plugin to Milk
docs.text:
Plugins in milk are external modules or compute units that extend its functionality without modifying the core codebase. They are automatically discovered and built thanks to milk's CMake configuration.

This guide outlines exactly how to create, structure, and link a custom plugin.

See also: Programmer's Guide · Code Assist Tools · Developer Tutorial · Build Tiers · Loading Modules

docs.title: 1. Where do plugins go?
docs.text:
All plugins belong inside the plugins/ directory at the root of the project. Milk's configuration script uses find -mindepth 2 -maxdepth 2 inside plugins/ to discover subdirectories containing a CMakeLists.txt.

Typically, plugins are placed inside an intermediate group folder such as:

  • plugins/milk-extra-src/<your_plugin>
  • plugins/cacao-src/<your_plugin> (For cacao AO loop modules)

Note

Because plugins are decoupled, it's very common for them to be their own isolated git repositories. You can add them under plugins/ via standard copying, as a git submodule, or even via symbolic links.

docs.title: Standalone Executables Relation to Core
docs.text: When a plugin registers a standalone executable (e.g., milk-fpsexec-myplugin), it behaves as a native Linux process that interacts with the core engine (streams and FPS) solely via shared memory. The plugin's calculation logic should NOT depend directly on internal GUI/CLI headers from CLIcore. By explicitly creating plugins and linking to _compute libraries, you ensure strict modularity where crashing plugins do not disrupt the orchestrating daemon.

docs.title: 2. Setting up CMakeLists.txt
docs.text:
When milk detects a CMakeLists.txt in your plugin's directory, it will automatically process it via add_subdirectory(). The file is expected to define your module's shared library and register its standalone executables.

Here is a standard template for a plugin's CMakeLists.txt:

# =======================================
# my_new_plugin - Short description
# =======================================

set(LIBNAME my_new_plugin)

# 1. Source files
set(SOURCEFILES 
    my_plugin_func.c
)

# 2. Shared Library (used by the interactive milk-cli)
add_library(${LIBNAME} SHARED ${SOURCEFILES})
target_link_libraries(${LIBNAME} PRIVATE CLIcore)

# 3. Compute-only variant (no CLI deps, for standalone executables linking it)
set(LIBNAME_COMPUTE ${LIBNAME}_compute)
add_library(${LIBNAME_COMPUTE} SHARED ${SOURCEFILES})
target_compile_definitions(${LIBNAME_COMPUTE} PRIVATE MILK_NO_CLI)
target_link_libraries(${LIBNAME_COMPUTE} PRIVATE milkdata ImageStreamIO)

# 4. Standalone Executable Definition
# This automatically handles the FPS lifecycle and links COREMOD_compute libs
add_milk_standalone(my_plugin_func my_plugin_func.c)

docs.title: 3. Writing the Source Code
docs.text:
From a source code standpoint, a plugin operates exactly like any standard core milk module.

Specifically, it should be written as a "compute unit" implementing the V2 FPS standard architecture. You must use the canonical template src/milk_module_example/examplefunc_fps_cli_poc.c as your starting point.

docs.title: Dual-Mode Headers Requirement
docs.text:
Plugins are often compiled twice: once for the shared library (CLI) and once for the standalone executable. To stay compliant and not violate dependency chains (i.e. to ensure standalones do not depend on graphical/TUI CLI elements), your C code must use conditional includes:

#ifdef MILK_NO_CLI
#include "CLIcore_standalone.h"   /* Stub types for standalone mode */
#else
#include "CLIcore.h"              /* Full CLI types for shared lib mode */
#endif
#include "fps.h"                  /* Always required for FPS structures */

docs.title: 4. Specialized Cacao Plugins
docs.text:
If you are writing a plugin specifically for the cacao AO loop, your standalone executable target is configured slightly differently.

Instead of add_milk_standalone, use add_cacao_standalone. This tells the build system to prefix your executable properly (e.g. cacao-fpsexec-myfunc).

# Minimal cacao standalone
add_cacao_standalone(my_cacao_func my_cacao_func.c)

# If your cacao standalone depends on code from other plugins (like fft or imagegen)
add_cacao_standalone_plugins(my_cacao_func my_cacao_func.c fft imagegen)

docs.title: 5. Reviewing the Build
docs.text:
Once your CMakeLists.txt and C sources are in progress:

  1. Navigate back to the main milk build directory.
  2. Run cmake ..
  3. Look for the message ADDING SUBDIR = plugins/milk-extra-src/my_new_plugin. If you see that, milk has successfully hooked your plugin into the global project.

docs.title: Developer Tutorial: Writing Your First Milk Module
docs.text:
Welcome to milk! This tutorial will guide you through creating your first module and standalone fpsexec compute block. By the end of this guide, you will have a working module linked to the milk core frameworks.

See also: Programmer's Guide · Code Assist Tools · Adding Plugins · FPS · FPS Standalone Modes

docs.title: 1. Setting Up the Directory Structure
docs.text:
The easiest way to start is by copying the provided example module. We will create a new module named my_first_module.

cd milk/plugins/milk-extra-src/
cp -r ../../src/milk_module_example my_first_module
cd my_first_module

docs.title: 2. Configuring CMake
docs.text:
Open CMakeLists.txt in your new directory. You need to identify your module and tell the build system which files to compile.

Change the LIBNAME to your module's name:

# Change this:
# set(LIBNAME milk_module_example)
set(LIBNAME my_first_module)

Define your source files and the standalone executables you want to build:

set(SOURCEFILES
    examplefunc.c
    examplefunc2_FPS.c
    # Add your own source files here
)

# Register a standalone executable
# add_milk_standalone(short_name source_file.c)
add_milk_standalone(my-first-exec examplefunc2_FPS.c)

docs.title: 3. Writing an FPS Compute Block
docs.text:
The Function Parameter Structure (FPS) is the standard way milk exposes configuration variables to the outside world (like the milk-fpsCTRL TUI).

Let's look at a basic FPS setup in my_first_module_fps.c. You need an info struct, a parameter mapping, and an execution loop.

docs.title: A. Define the Application Info
docs.text:
Every fpsexec program needs an ID string, a command key, and a short description:

#include "fps.h"

FPS_APP_INFO FPS_app_info = {
    .fps_name = "myfirstexec", // SHM name on disk
    .cmdkey = "myexec",        // CLI keyword
    .description = "My very first milk compute block!"
};

docs.title: B. Map Parameters
docs.text:
Use the FPS_PARAMS X-Macro to define the configuration parameters you want to expose:

// Local Variables
static int32_t param_iterations = 100;
static float   param_gain = 0.5f;

// Parameter mapping (X-macro)
#define FPS_PARAMS(X) \
    X(".iterations", &param_iterations, \
      FPTYPE_INT32, 1, \
      FPFLAG_DEFAULT_INPUT, "Number of iterations") \
    X(".gain", &param_gain, \
      FPTYPE_FLOAT32, 1, \
      FPFLAG_DEFAULT_INPUT, "Loop gain")

docs.title: C. Implement the Compute Function
docs.text:
This is the core compute function. It is called after parameters are synced from FPS shared memory.

static errno_t fpsexec(void) {
    printf("Running with gain %f, %d iterations\n",
           param_gain, param_iterations);

    for (int i = 0; i < param_iterations; i++) {
        // Do math here...
    }

    return RETURN_SUCCESS;
}

docs.title: D. The Main Entry Point
docs.text:
The V2 macro generates the standalone main() function that handles the FPS lifecycle (create, exec, confstart, runstart, etc.):

// Processinfo-wrapped entry point
static errno_t compute_function() {
    INSERT_STD_PROCINFO_COMPUTEFUNC_START
    fpsexec();
    INSERT_STD_PROCINFO_COMPUTEFUNC_END
    return RETURN_SUCCESS;
}

// Standalone main (compiled with -DFPS_STANDALONE)
#ifdef FPS_STANDALONE
FPS_MAIN_STANDALONE_V2(FPS_app_info, FPS_PARAMS, compute_function)
#endif

docs.title: 4. Compile and Run!
docs.text:
Go back to the root milk directory and re-run standard compilation. CMake will automatically discover your newly linked plugin.

cd ../../../
bash compile.sh $PWD/local

Now, launch your standalone FPS compute block!

milk-fpsexec-my-first-exec -tmux

Open a new terminal and inspect your running parameter tree:

milk-fpsCTRL myfirstexec

Congratulations! You've successfully written a milk module and an FPS compute block.

docs.title: Build Tiers
docs.text:
Note

The milk build system supports multiple build tiers, controlled by CMake options. Lower tiers have fewer external dependencies and produce a smaller footprint.

docs.title: CMake Options
docs.text:
Option Default Description USE_COREMODS ON Build core modules (COREMOD_*) USE_CFITSIO ON Build FITS I/O (requires cfitsio) USE_CLI ON Build interactive CLI (milk-cli) USE_NCURSES ON Enable ncurses / TUI screens USE_READLINE ON Enable readline for CLI input USE_GSL ON Enable GSL for plugins

Important

Dependency chain:

  • USE_CLI=ON automatically enables USE_COREMODS
  • Plugins are only built when USE_COREMODS=ON
  • USE_CFITSIO=OFF excludes COREMOD_iofits and compiles remaining modules without cfitsio linkage

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
Tier cmake command What you get Engine cmake .. -DUSE_COREMODS=OFF -DUSE_CLI=OFF ImageStreamIO, processinfo, FPS, standalone tools Core cmake .. -DUSE_CLI=OFF -DUSE_CFITSIO=OFF + COREMOD_arith, memory, tools (no cfitsio) Core + FITS cmake .. -DUSE_CLI=OFF + COREMOD_iofits (requires cfitsio) Full cmake .. + CLI, all plugins, example module Full + CUDA cmake .. -DUSE_CUDA=ON + GPU acceleration

All tiers are built with:

$ mkdir _build && cd _build
$ cmake .. [OPTIONS]        # see table above
$ make -j$(nproc)
$ sudo make install

docs.title: Behavior When cfitsio Is Disabled
docs.text:
When built with USE_CFITSIO=OFF, FITS-dependent code paths are compiled out via #ifdef USE_CFITSIO guards:

Module Effect COREMOD_iofits Not built — iofits.loadfits / iofits.saveFITS unavailable COREMOD_memory logshmim, saveall, stream_pixmapdecode print a warning instead of writing FITS COREMOD_arith No impact (never used cfitsio) COREMOD_tools No impact

Tip

The engine and core tiers are ideal for embedded or real-time deployments where only shared-memory stream processing is needed and disk I/O to FITS files is unnecessary.

docs.title: 1. Download and install milk
docs.text:
Warning

This page describes installation of the core package milk. If you install an application package (cacao or coffee), replace "milk" with "cacao" in these instructions.

For download, build commands, and CMake options, see the Quick Start section in README.md.

For configuring minimal or partial builds (engine-only, core without cfitsio, etc.), see Build Tiers.

The sections below cover post-installation setup, dependencies, and optional configuration not covered in the README.

docs.title: 2. Post-installation
docs.text:
You may need to add /usr/local/lib to the linker search path:

$ echo "/usr/local/lib" > usrlocal.conf
$ sudo mv usrlocal.conf /etc/ld.so.conf.d/
$ sudo ldconfig -v

docs.title: 3. tmpfs (optional)
docs.text:
Create a tmpfs disk for high-performance shared-memory I/O:

$ echo "tmpfs /milk/shm tmpfs rw,nosuid,nodev" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
$ sudo mkdir -p /milk/shm
$ sudo mount /milk/shm

docs.title: 4.1. Required (full build)
docs.text:
Dependency Purpose gcc C compiler (C17) cmake ≥ 3.10 Build system pkg-config Locates installed libraries pthreads POSIX threading (provided by libc) Optional dependencies Package installation commands

Ubuntu / Debian:

$ sudo apt-get install \
    libcfitsio-dev libreadline-dev libncurses5-dev \
    libfftw3-dev libgsl-dev

CentOS / RHEL / Fedora:

$ sudo yum install \
    cfitsio-devel readline-devel ncurses-devel \
    fftw3-devel gsl-devel
cfitsio from source (alternative)

If your distribution does not package cfitsio, install it from source:

  1. Download from HEASARC
  2. Build and install:
$ tar xzf cfitsio-*.tar.gz
$ cd cfitsio-*
$ ./configure --prefix=/usr/local
$ make
$ sudo make install
GPU acceleration (optional)

For GPU-accelerated linear algebra:

  • Install NVIDIA driver and CUDA toolkit
  • Install MAGMA

If cmake reports "No package 'magma' found", add the MAGMA pkg-config path to your shell profile:

export PKG_CONFIG_PATH=/usr/local/magma/lib/pkgconfig
Running multiple versions side by side

⚠️ Warning: Untested — may require tweaking.

Install independent versions by specifying different prefixes:

$ cd ~/src
$ git clone --recursive https://github.com/milk-org/milk milk-1
$ git clone --recursive https://github.com/milk-org/milk milk-2

$ cd ~/src/milk-1/_build
$ cmake -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr/local/milk-1 ..
$ sudo make install

$ cd ~/src/milk-2/_build
$ cmake -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr/local/milk-2 ..
$ sudo make install

Make version 1 the system default:

$ sudo ln -s /usr/local/milk-1 /usr/local/milk

Run version 2 explicitly:

$ LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/milk-2/lib \
  PATH=/usr/local/milk-2/bin \
  milk-cli

Each version can also use its own shared-memory directory:

$ MILK_SHM_DIR=/milk-2/shm \
  LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/milk-2/lib \
  PATH=/usr/local/milk-2/bin \
  milk-cli
